utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom. I see you on your feet, Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours, and good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom. I just have two brief issues that I would like to raise, housekeeping, and they both relate to interpretation. We've received, actually, translated documents, the documents that had earlier been MFI'd, and we believe that now they can be fully admitted into evidence. If you allow me, I would like to read out the numbers. There are five documents in total. That's D195, D215, D231, D257, and D261. The next issue that I wanted to raise is actually some information. The CLSS service refused to translate certain documents from English into B/C/S, into Serbian, documents that the Defence intends to use with this witness, Mr. Butler. The document that I'm talking about is on our 65 ter list under 1D924, and we can all see it now in the courtroom. And I believe that we will need your assistance in order for the CLSS to translate this document. I would just like to say as a preface that all of the documents that are admitted into evidence that we are going to use are both in English and Serbian. However, to my surprise, we were informed by the CLSS service that documents are only translated into official languages of this Tribunal; in other words, from Serbian into English, but not the other way around. It is my belief, however, that this Trial Chamber has made a ruling - it was a while back - that all documents that have to be used in the courtroom have to be translated into B/C/S as well. I would just like to read out the Registry translation policy out of that document. That's paragraph 1.4, and it reads: [In English] "Self-represented accused should submit a request for translation of evidence into B/C/S, and where there is no order from a Chamber resolving the question of requests to translate material into B/C/S, the matter will be referred to the deputy chief of CMSS, in the first instance, or the chief of CMSS, if required, and the decision to grant or refuse the request will be agreed upon in a consultation with the chief of CLSS." [Interpretation] Now, since we've already had documents translated from English into Serbian, especially those documents that are submitted by the Prosecution, we believe that the Defence should be treated the same way and that documents that we are tendering into evidence should also be translated. And if, in the future, the Defence had to take upon itself the burden of translating all the documents that we are going to use into Serbian, it would be a tremendous load that we can barely manage. We have done so so far, and we've even translated parts of the transcript, the relevant parts, of course, so far, and there will be just a small number of documents that we intend to tender into evidence that we will request to be translated by the CLSS. The document I'm talking about is 1D924, and this Defence considers this document very important. It relates to the convoys and the UNPROFOR position, and this is the document that CLSS refused to translate. So in conclusion, we would like your assistance to order CLSS to translate this document, 1D924, as soon as possible into Serbian. And, two, if we could have the CLSS informed of the practice in this case, the practice that applies to the Prosecution but that should apply to the Defence as well, and that relates to the translation of documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Gajic. Does the Prosecution take a position on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's a strange-sounding situation. I can't imagine why the CLSS can't translate a UN cable, and I think it should be translated. But aside from that, we would stay out of it. I think, of course, the Defence should be able to have English documents of reasonable length that are relevant translated by CLSS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. It is a serious matter. The Chamber will inquire the background of this conflict and this problem, and we will come back to that matter as soon as possible. In relation to the five documents which have now a translation into English, the first one, D195, was not only marked for identification because of a lack of a translation, but also because the witness, Rupert Smith, was not in a position to testify about the content and to authenticate this document. That happened on the 28th of March this year. Therefore, this document will remain MFI'd. The others, D215, D231, D257, and D261, will now be exhibits in this trial. If there are no other matters to deal with before the witness comes back into the courtroom, he should be brought in, please. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe that you're absolutely right. It was my error regarding document D195. And I see the note that I made myself at the time, but I believe that I just made an omission, in view of the other problems we have. Now, if I can just add one more thing before the witness comes in. You've already seen that we have already 200 days, and in view of the fact that the Defence did not frequently raise issues, such as the one that I raised earlier on, and that we were very efficient in dealing with all documents, regardless of what language they were in, we would really now urge the Trial Chamber to assist us, because if we are unable to obtain documents in translation that are required, this may affect the length of the trial, itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, I think we understood your position, and we take it very seriously and will deal with that immediately. Welcome back, and good afternoon, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Again, the affirmation to tell the truth still applies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey is continuing his examination-in-chief. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And could we go back to P13, Vinko Pandurevic's interim combat report of 15 July, where we left off. It should be in tab 167.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just to remind us, you'd testified that the first three paragraphs updated the urgent military situation that Pandurevic was facing. Then you gave us your analysis of the statement: "The additional burden for us is the large number of prisoners distributed throughout schools in the brigade area, as well as obligations of security and "restoration of the terrain," or "asanacija terena," as it's in the Serbian. And then the next paragraph states: "This command cannot take care of these problems any longer, as it has neither the material or other resources. If no one takes on this responsibility, I will be forced to let them go." What do you think this is a reference to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, it has two possible meanings. The first one could be related to the column that is going through. The second one could be related to the issue of prisoners being detained in the schools that were still being detained at this time, although I think the second one is more or less an empty threat, because I can't see somebody such as Colonel Pandurevic effectively releasing 1500 prisoners kilometres behind his own front-lines and deep within his rear area and somehow expecting that they're going to make their way out of his territory into friendly territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Have you -- personally have your own opinion on which of these two possibilities is the appropriate one?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not believe he's discussing the column here. It is my view that he is making a threat, albeit an empty one, to his superiors related to the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. In the three previous paragraphs, where he talks about the situation, and the forces of the -- the Muslim forces, and the attack that's still progressing, is there any mention at all of the possibility of opening a corridor or allowing any of these Muslims through these lines? Is there any suggestion there in those first three paragraphs?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. And, in part, this is why I believe that in the particular context of how this document is written, that Pandurevic is taking the phrase "forced to let them go" and it's referring to the prisoners being detained at the schools in his municipality and not as a result of what's happening with the column.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In any of these three paragraphs that we see, the first three paragraphs, or, indeed, the situation in the battle-field at the time, is there any indication that at that point that he's writing this, that Pandurevic actually has some kind of control over or the ability over the Muslims in the woods that are coming in large numbers through his zone?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he believes he does. He talks about the fact, for example, in the third paragraph, that despite having no reserves, that they have sealed off various areas pertaining to the column. And further down, there is -- I guess it's paragraph 7, just a one-sentence paragraph, he reiterates that while the situation is complicated, it's under control.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. This next paragraph: "I made an offer to the commander of the other side to separate out the civilians and have the others surrender, but he refused, asking that they should all be released together." How do you analyse this comment in relation to this interpretation of the rest of the document that you've just talked about?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this particular context, as we've heard before, there have been references to ongoing communication between Semso Muminovic - I hope I've pronounced that correctly - who was leading Muslim military attacks from the ABiH 2 Corps in an effort to relieve pressure and open a hole for the column to get through, and members of the Zvornik Brigade, to include Colonel Pandurevic when he arrived back there on the early morning -- or in the morning hours of 15 July. Colonel Pandurevic had earlier, at that 1200 meeting with other commanders of the MUP and his own subordinates, ruled out completely letting the column go, and in this particular comment he's making it clear that, you know, he's still not prepared to let the column go in the context that it is, but he's holding open the possibility and laying out his position that, you know, he would accept some kind of agreement where, under some circumstances, the column stops, a cease-fire is declared, and the Zvornik Brigade has the ability to essentially separate those individuals who are members of the former 28th Division from those individuals who are considered to somehow be civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So if that's correct, this paragraph: "I made an offer to the commander ...," is still indicating a refusal to let even the civilians through. When we look at the paragraph above: "I will let the column go ...," is that in contradiction to that, meaning to suggest that "let them go" is the column or consistent with it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it contradicts the idea that at this point in time, Colonel Pandurevic is prepared to let the entire column go. I believe what it's accurately discussing is the fact that he's not prepared to let the column go because he's not prepared to accept military personnel in the column escaping, in conjunction with civilians who are believed to be in the column.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And to remind us, does that situation for Pandurevic change a bit later, just to remind us of what happens a bit later, and when, how far later?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on military activity that occurs throughout, primarily, the evening hours of the 15th of July, and the early-morning hours of the 16th of July, at some point in the morning or early afternoon of the 16th of July, Colonel Pandurevic changes his view on this subject and believes that the casualties that the Muslim column is inflicting on his particular units are greater than the benefits that his unit is getting for engaging the column, and that he, again without proper authorisation, makes a decision to allow the entire column, to include combatants and civilians, pass through his lines. He does declare that cease-fire 24 hours later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And taking you back briefly to Borovcanin's after-action report, where he describes being present in the Batkovica [phoen] area and the Muslims taking Serbs weapons and turning them on the Serbs, do you relate that description by Borovcanin to anything that you've just described that Pandurevic was concerned about when he changed his mind to open a corridor?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I believe that Colonel Pandurevic's understanding of the situation on 16 July reflects his belief that at that time, his particular brigade, I mean, specifically the 4th Infantry Battalion and the 6th Infantry Battalion, have been particularly hard hit by the column. In fact, the morning of the 16th of July, the 4th Battalion headquarters and command post is actually over-run by the column, resulting in a number of casualties. At the same time, the evening of the 15th and the morning of the 16th, the Zvornik Brigade loses contact with a unit of soldiers that had come up from Bratunac and were literally lost in the woods, and there was fear that this particular unit had, in fact, been wiped out by the column. It later surfaced that they had just been lost and out of radio contact. So when one looks at the battle-field from Colonel Pandurevic's eyes on the 16th of July, it is clear that he sees an extremely complex situation and a situation that is increasingly causing casualties within his units, and I believe it is in that light that he makes the decision ultimately to allow the column to pass.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, let me take you back to this document. And you've described obligations of security, in your view, mean guarding of the prisoners, and "restoration of the terrain," or as it's said in the original, "asanacija terena," what is your understanding of both the meaning of "asanacija" and the use of the term of "asanacija" as we see it in these documents? Is it the same, is it different?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The phrase "asanacija" is, from its translation in various military and military medical regulations of the former SFRY, simply a description of the processes that occur where biological hazard material is cleared and disposed of because of the risk of disease to humans. It can be simply something when the military will go into a disaster area and remove livestock that has been killed by some calamity because you can't leave them on a -- you know, a piece of land or real estate because of the threat of disease. It would also include a process of going over a former battle-field that you now control, collecting the dead and burying them. It is simply a military sanitation term.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how do you believe it is -- you've already explained what you believe it means here. What do you believe it means here, and have you seen this term used other ways in these documents, or similar ways?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've seen the term used in similar documents related to this always describing the burial of human remains. In this particular document, it is my view that the only thing that Colonel Pandurevic can be talking about here is the burial of Bosnian Muslim prisoners who have been executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, you have, yourself, described that there was fighting going on on the 14th, in the woods, as the approach towards Baljkovica, the 15th around Baljkovica, as you've just described. Could this be a reference to going in and cleaning up the battle-field from that combat?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a practical matter, one usually waits until the conclusion of combat activities before attempting to bury the bodies of individuals killed in combat. When one looks at the dates that the military attacks were taking place on the 13th and the 14th and the 15th, there's still active combat going on in these locations. It's not practical that the VRS, while they are engaged in combat, in some places on terrain that they don't control, is going to engage in efforts to bury Muslim members of the column who were killed as part of the combat operations. They're certainly not going to be burying Bosnian Serb soldiers on the battle-field in that sense. So when one looks at this phrase and what's happening on the battle-field, it makes no sense that they would be burying battle casualties in that sense. When you couple this with the military engineer records of the Zvornik Brigade, which actually shows where various earth-moving machines are in operation and, in fact, it coincides with locations of mass executions, I believe it becomes quite clear exactly what he was using this phrase in context with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to the next document. It's 65 ter 143, and this is also an interim combat report, but this time from the Drina Corps to the Main Staff. It's in the name of the commander, General Krstic, and I think any review of this document will show that while it does discuss some attack, there's certainly no reference of Pandurevic having the burden of guarding large numbers of prisoners in schools in his area and his obligation to bury them or do "asanacija." So this information, this is not -- what Pandurevic said to the Drina Corps in his interim report does not appear to be going up through the official interim report of the Drina Corps to the Main Staff if it had been received at this time. Would you expect in this report, or in a later report if the timing didn't coincide, that the Drina Corps would actually communicate in writing similar information that Pandurevic sent to them about guarding and burying large numbers of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regardless of the timing, I would not expect that the Drina Corps, in its reporting, would report that fact, the security obligations and the "asanacija," to its higher command. Clearly, you know, on two occasions, because of circumstances and the pressure that he's under, Colonel Pandurevic makes these written references in his reports to the Drina Corps, in part, expressing his frustration about the circumstances that he's in the middle of, and on the 18th, you know, seeking to justify his decisions. General Krstic, in this context, isn't feeling that same pressure and frustration, and certainly wouldn't feel that he'd want to put this in writing to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to the next document. I'm sorry, this does need to be placed into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 143 shall be assigned Exhibit P2545. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And here at P479, we're back to our chronology and we're back to the Zepa area, a document from General Tolimir, from the Rogatica Brigade area, dated 15 July, to the Security Department of the 1st Krajina Corps, and he is talking about the provision of a loud-speaker to be transported to the Rogatica Garrison by 1500 hours on 16 July. Do you have any idea what this is about?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the context of this document, it appears that General Tolimir believes that through the use of, essentially, loud-speakers to transmit propaganda or other messages to the Bosnian Muslim military garrison or military units around Zepa, that he can potentially weaken their resolve to resist or, in fact, even induce them into surrendering in some numbers by promising that they will be cared for, fed, and treated in accordance with the relevant conventions. So this is the technical aspect of him seeking to obtain the relevant equipment that he needs in order to accomplish this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What, if anything, does General Tolimir communicating over this means indicate about his whereabouts and his availability to those that would seek him out to provide him with information?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is generally a reflection that he can be found in and around the command post of the 1st Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade; if not personally there at all times, certainly as a place where messages can be sent and then they will be relayed to him, wherever he happens to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's get over to the 16th now and go to P845A. Actually, before we get there, I'd like to go to a document that you suggested yesterday. It is the duty officer -- the list of the duty officer of the Drina Corps, and the number for that is 2202. And we're going to have to just look at the screen. I think it's something I removed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Are you referring to P2202?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it's 65 ter 2202, and the other one is 2203. It's a two-part document, but if we could start with 2202.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I think yesterday you were trying to recollect who was the duty officer from the Drina Corps at various times. And if we could blow that up, especially the English, for Mr. Butler to take a look at. And we're interested in the days of -- if we could get 17 across the top in. There we go. That's helpful. I think you mentioned Mr. Cerovic. So can you tell us what this -- first of all, what this document is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This particular document looks to be a list of various officers of the Drina Corps, reflecting their name and rank, and then what corresponding days they are scheduled to perform duty in the Operations Centre of the Drina Corps Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so according to this, who would have been the duty officer on July 16th, 1995?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I read this -- it just disappeared. If I read this correctly, it would be a Lieutenant Colonel Rakic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And if we look at Cerovic all the way across the month, do we see him ever holding the duty officer job?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Can you remind us who Cerovic is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Cerovic at this time is the assistant commander for Morale, Legal, and Religious Affairs for the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I would offer this document in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And this is 65 ter 2202; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Because you were referring to two different numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That one's coming next.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes. This will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 2202 shall be assigned Exhibit P2546. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if we could put 2203 up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this, you'll be able to see, is the list of assistants to the duty officer at the Drina Corps. And can you tell us just very briefly - I believe the Court's heard it before - but how does this work, the duty officer and his assistant?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The duty officer and the assistant, during their performance of duty, their scheduled performance of duty, are the focal point by which most issues will come into a particular unit or headquarters, and it is their responsibility to accept the incoming task, lay the task out, and make that initial decision as to where the task should go within the command in order to be properly dealt with. Most of the issues that the duty officers deal with are the usual routine things that come into the command. The one issue that is of note is that in the event that decisions need to be made and the commander, or deputy commander, or other relevant officers who would be in the chain of command are not available, the duty officer is authorised to undertake those limited decisions in light of what he understands the commander's guidance is. So because of these various duties, the duty officer is someone, as well as his assistant, who are always in and around the Operations Centre and have a very detailed awareness of the situation that's occurring in their particular unit or headquarters during the period that they're performing the duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Practically, who do you normally see writing notes in the middle of the night? How did it practically work in that respect between duty officer and assistant duty officer?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Practically speaking, the duty officer would usually try and catch a few hours of sleep, and the assistant duty officer would be the guy left awake to manage the activities. Having said that, the duty officer is not going home. If he's sleeping, he's sleeping on a cot where he can be, you know, woken up and brought into the situation within a minute or two. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I'd offer this document into evidence as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 2203 shall be assigned Exhibit P2547. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And now let's go to P845A. This is in 170, the tab, and it's a 16 July intercept between Colonel Ljubo Beara, Cerovic, and X.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I take it this is the same Ljubo Beara you've been talking about.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who do you believe this Cerovic is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe this is Colonel Cerovic, the assistant commander for Morale, Legal and Religious Affairs for the Drina Corps. And I guess I should note in this context, from my earlier testimony, based on the previous exhibits, he was not performing his duty officer -- he was not performing as the duty officer, so I previously misspoke there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where do you believe Beara is and where do you believe Cerovic is, based on this conversation and the other information?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given the time and date that it's occurring, I believe that Colonel Beara is at the Zvornik Brigade headquarters and that Colonel Cerovic is at the Drina Corps Command in Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we see this, that Cerovic says: "Hey, listen to me. Triage has to be done today ... taken prisoners." X says: "Yes." There's some distortion. X says: "To do triage." Cerovic says: "Triage has to be done on the prisoners." X says: "Colonel Beara is right here by me." Cerovic says: "Give me Beara." X says: "Go ahead." B, would be for "Beara," says: "Yes." Cerovic says: "Ljubo." Beara says: "I hear you." Cerovic says: "Hello. Cerovic speaking." What, in your view, is this triage that has to be done on prisoners? First of all, what prisoners do you think Cerovic is talking about here at 1111 hours on 16 July?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: On 16 July, the last clusters of prisoners are those at the Pilica School and in the Dom of Culture.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so what do you make "triage" to mean in this context?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't take it to believe [sic] that it's being done in the medical sense. Neither Colonel Beara or Colonel Cerovic are obviously medical personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Remind us in an army, what -- in an army combat situation, what "triage" means.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a military medical sense, triage is a battle-field medical evaluation whereas military medical personnel prioritise wounded soldiers or other personnel in terms of the ability to treat them and the timeliness of their treatment, generally identifies those wounded who will survive their wounds without immediate care and then can be placed off to the side, it identifies those individuals who, without immediate care, would or could die of their wounds, and, further, it identifies individuals who are wounded so grievously that it might be that despite any medical care given to them, they're not expected to survive their wounds. In a battle-field context, military medicine is not unlimited, and sometimes those types of difficult choices have to be made in light of the circumstances and the availability of qualified medical personnel to treat the wounded. So those -- that decision process and the procedures associated with it are generally known as "triage."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Have you had a chance to review the witness statements or testimony of survivors that were held at the Pilica School, in terms of whether or not they received any medical help or any significant amount of food or water?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding of their both statements and testimony over the years is that they did not receive life support in the sense of food, appreciable amounts of water, or any medical care whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So what do you think "triage" means in this context?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this particular document, my opinion is that "triage" is a euphemistic phrase that they're using to say the prisoners need to be taken out and executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How do you make that conclusion? What do you base that on?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: When this document originally came into -- or when this intercept originally came into the possession of the Office of the Prosecutor, we did -- certainly I did, obviously, look into the circumstances to determine whether or not it could have another meaning related to military medicine. Through the course of the investigation, and when one looks at this in context with other intercepts, other documents, and the events that are occurring on the ground at the time, it becomes clear that it could be the only thing that he's talking about. They're not medical personnel. And in light of the fact that the -- now the only known wounded prisoners are those 13 or 15 that are in the Standard facility, I don't believe that Colonel Beara and Colonel Cerovic are referring to them. Those individuals have already been treated, and they are essentially recovering from their injuries at the Standard facility. And as discussed earlier, there are other intercepts and documents and testimony related to what really happened to those particular individuals at a later date. So putting all of this together, in light of what was happening in the circumstances, that is what I base my conclusion on that the subject that they are talking about is murdering the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Continuing, Cerovic says: "Cerovic speaking." You see that in the middle. Beara says: "I hear you." Cerovic says: "Trkulja --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I interrupt you for a moment, because Judge Mindua has a question to the last part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. McCloskey, I have a short question for you. I'm looking for the document in question. Yesterday, we talked about -- I have the document now. Witness, yesterday, in document 65 ter 249, which was admitted into evidence and received the Exhibit P2544, we saw in this exhibit that Colonel Vidoje Blagojevic say that there were children -- at least four children aged between eight and fourteen among the detainees, the prisoners. We are now, in the document we have before us, reviewing this document, and you have provided us with an explanation for the term "triage." You indicated that this term could not refer to people who were ill or wounded. What do you think of these children who were among the detainees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, sir, in the context of where these events were happening on the battle-field, the four children were part of a group that was captured on, I believe, the 17th of July, 1995, based on that sweep operation that was jointly accomplished by the military and MUP units, and, yes, sir, you're correct in that sense. A decision was made by somebody that these four children would be culled from that group of prisoners and taken to Bratunac. And I guess the fate of the remaining adults that were captured as part of that has been the subject of testimony that I'm not too familiar with. In this particular context, this is a conversation that is occurring on the 16th of July, 1995. There are only two groups of prisoners that would be of potential topic of discussion between these two officers. The first group of prisoners are those who are detained in the facilities at Pilica and the Dom of Culture. The only other group of potential prisoners would be individuals who might have surrendered from the column to members of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade and the other police units that were fighting at Baljkovica, Memici, and those locations. Unfortunately, as the investigation has borne out, in almost all of those cases where prisoners are taken as a result of being captured from the column in the Zvornik area, most of them are relatively quickly executed. They don't survive long enough to be separated or triaged in that sense anywhere else. So it's because of these circumstances, again related to my understanding of the circumstances as they're occurring on the ground, that I draw the conclusion that what Colonel Beara and that what Colonel Cerovic are talking about are the execution of those prisoners still held at Pilica, in the school, and at the Dom of Culture. Those are the final large grouping of prisoners in the Zvornik Brigade area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And just as a follow-up on that: The four children that were picked up in the sweep operation, where was that in relation to the Zvornik area schools that you're talking about all those prisoners in the schools were on the 16th? Excuse me, the Kula School and the Cultural Centre.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Particularly the Kula School and the Cultural Centre are located in the 1st Battalion of the Zvornik Brigade area, to the extreme north end of the Zvornik municipality. The prisoners captured as part of the sweep operation -- or the four children, I should say, captured as part of the sweep operation the next day are those captured in the woods near Konjevic Polje, which puts them in the Bratunac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And to make sure it's clear, do you -- are you aware of the fate of those four children? Was that something that was determined, in your recollection, as part of your time here?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that particular aspect of the investigation was completed after I left. But if I recall correctly, I understand that those four children did, in fact, survive, if I recall it correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, I think it's -- the Defence would not object if I did tell you that, yes, those children did, in fact, survive and had been interviewed. So that's perfectly clear for the record, if I'd not made that clear sooner.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, Beara says: "I hear you." And then Cerovic says: "Trkulja was here with me just now, and he was looking for you. I don't know." Who do you take this "Trkulja" to be?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the same Colonel Trkulja who is the chief of armour and mechanised forces on the Main Staff, and his name, of course, is mentioned in the 17 July 1995 Main Staff order as one of the three officers who was sent the next day to the Zvornik Brigade to determine what happened with respect to the column.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So if Cerovic is at the Drina Corps headquarters in Vlasenica and says that, Trkulja was here with me, what does that suggest to you where Trkulja was on the 16th?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That on the 16th he had travelled from the Main Staff to Vlasenica and was present in the Drina Corps headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And Beara says: "Yes." Cerovic says: "So he told me ... he got instructions from above." What do you think this means? Who are they talking about?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people above Trkulja, as a Main Staff officer, would be his senior leaders of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And then Beara says: "Yes." Cerovic says: "To do triage on those --" And then he's interrupted. Beara says: "I don't want to talk about it on the phone." What do you take that comment to mean?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's as before, Colonel Beara, among many others, understood that these lines were subject to intercept by hostile forces. It's something, again, I use not as a throw-away line, but as a reflection of the fact that if we were really discussing a legitimate issue of medical triage, one wouldn't think that that would be a particularly sensitive issue that Colonel Beara would feel a compelling need to cut somebody off on the phone to remind them that these issues shouldn't be discussed over this potential phone line.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to the next document, P846. It's another 16 July intercept a little bit later now in the afternoon. It's 1358 hours.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This confidential document should not be broadcast. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's from the Zlatar duty officer and the Palma duty officer, and the Palma duty officer says: "Hello, Zlatar. Give me the duty officer." Just remind us again, what's "Zlatar" and "Palma"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Zlatar" is the telephonic code-name for the Drina Corps Command. "Palma "is the telephonic code-name for the Zvornik Brigade Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And the Palma duty officer says: "500 litres of D2 for Lieutenant Colonel Popovic." And then Zlatar says: "For Lieutenant Colonel Popovic?" Palma says: "Yes." Then apparently the line disconnects, and it starts up again, and there's reference to a Basevic. And Palma says: "Hello, is that Basevic?" And then B says: "Yes, it is." Do you know a Basevic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Who would that have been, in your view?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Major Basevic was an officer of the Drina Corps Command who worked in the Rear Services or Logistics Department.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And it goes on, and it says -- Palma says: "Lieutenant Colonel Popovic is here at Palma, you know." What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, taking what we know "Palma" stands for, it's a -- the correspondent essentially reporting that Colonel Popovic is at the headquarters of the Zvornik Brigade or at least in the Zvornik Brigade area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. It goes on to repeat that: "Popovic is at Palma." And then Palma goes on and says: "500 litres of D2 are urgently being asked for him or else the work he's doing will stop." Basevic says: "Well, fuck him, don't you have 500 litres of oil? They're asking for two tons loaded." On 16 July at 1358 hours, what do you believe Popovic's work is, as referenced in this intercept?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My opinion is that his work is related to the transportation of the Bosnian Muslim men from the school in Pilica to the site at Branjevo Farm where they're subsequently being executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, let's go on a bit, and we'll ask you how you come to that. But we see that Palma says: "Well, I don't know. He just called me from the field and told me to pass you the message over there." What do you make of that, "he called me from the field"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That line further notes that he's not physically standing or in the brigade headquarters at the time, but that he is passed a message through another means to the Zvornik Brigade, in this context the duty officer, to make his request through Palma, the Zvornik Brigade Command, to the Drina Corps for action.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is that consistent where you believe he is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, in the context of what's happening on the ground and where I believe he is, which would be in the 1st Battalion area, in the Zvornik Brigade area, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's turn the page to the next page in the English. And it's talking about: "Two tonnes are arriving now at your place. You can't find oil." It says: "Should I deliver by helicopter?" It says: "Well, then get in touch with Rocevic." Do you know what that -- is there any idea what that means, "Rocevic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether it's referring to an individual or a place. I'm not familiar, off-hand, with an officer named Rocevic, but it has been a few years.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. It goes down, and Palma says: "Yes, I did, and who is that, is that the duty officer?" And then C says: "The switchboard." Then Palma says: "Give me the operations duty officer." It says: "Is Major Golic there by chance?" C says: "Yes." Palma says: "Let me talk to him." Now, Palma is now saying: "Golic, Pop just called me and told me to contact you. 500 litres of D2 have to be sent to him immediately; otherwise, his work will stop." "Pop," what do you think that means, or who is -- what's that a reference to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Pop" is a nickname that is often associated with Colonel Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And again there's another reference that his work will stop. We see: "Yeah, man. Yeah, 500 litres, or else his work will stop. Go on, right away." "G," which would be "Golic," says: "Bye." So Golic, which Golic do you think this is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is, I believe, Major Golic, one of the intelligence officers from the Drina Corps Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And then another conversation starts off with Palma and: "A bus loaded with oil is to go to Pilica village. That's it." X says: "500 litres?" P says: "No, it should go with its fuel tank from the vehicle battalion." Now, this reference to Pilica, how do you fit that into your conclusion of what Popovic is doing and where?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the context of activities related to prisoners, on the 16th of July there are only two primary activities. One is the continued efforts to bury the bodies from the prisoners who are at Rocevic and who are killed in Kozluk. The second one is the process that occurs throughout the morning and day, where the prisoners are being taken from the Pilica School to Branjevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, this is 1358 hours on the 16th, and you have described what you had learned of the fierce combat at Batkovica. And I think you had mentioned and the Court has heard that a corridor got opened up at about that time, and here we have fuel taken to Pilica. Can you relate to us whether or not this fuel and Popovic could be related to these combat activities that are clearly a part of this case now that are going on at Baljkovica?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They're not related. Simply, when one looks at a map, which, of course, I don't have, and looks at the terrain and the locations of where the column is going out, and going through the 7th, 4th, and 6th Battalions out to ABiH-held territory, and then one looks at where the 1st Battalion in Pilica is, it's quite clear that they are geographically separated by a number of kilometres, perhaps 20 kilometres, and that would be straight line almost. When one looks at the terrain features and the ruggedness of the terrain, it's evident that the activities that are occurring in Pilica at that time can have absolutely no relationship to the military activities that are occurring in Memici and Baljkovica related to the column.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just to remind us, can we go to P2291, which is an illustrated map that is actually to scale and may give us some help in that regard. And if we could just put it up just to cover the whole page. Is it possible to blow it up one more? Yes, thank you. That's helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, first of all, can you remind us where the column of Muslims is going?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, and I guess I can mark up with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Wait one second. And we actually -- there -- okay, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: One will note, at the bottom of the map, the series of red lines [marks] which are depictions of the general route of the column and the various units that are impacted; the 7th Battalion, the 4th Battalion and the 6th Battalion [marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let me just stop. For the record, have you outlined the red lines in red, and you underlined the various battalions. Can you tell us, is this map one that was done in your time, do you recall?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And is this accurate, as far as you know, as to the approximate locations of the battalions and the route of the column?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. This particular map graphic is derived from a much more complex and detailed military map that was seized by the Office of the Prosecutor from the headquarters of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade, which laid out the route of the column as well as the areas and the defence lines of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade as they looked in July of 1995. So I'm familiar with the basic map that these particular graphics are derived from.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. And that military map is in evidence, Mr. President and Your Honours. I believe we provided you a hard copy of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could you underline "Pilica" for us that you think is the "Pilica" referred to in that intercept that we just had up there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. If one then goes from where these locations are, the 7th and the 4th and the 6th Battalion, which are the southern areas of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade, and goes all the way north -- to the extreme northern end of the Zvornik Brigade, one sees the 1st Battalion and, even further to the east, the complex of the school at Kula, and Pilica, and Branjevo [marks]. So it is based on that particular situation, and understanding this, that I conclude that the activities that are occurring in Pilica, Kula, and Branjevo cannot be related to military activities that are occurring against the column much further to the south-west.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would offer this drawn map, where he has circled the area up north in the 1st Battalion and the Pilica Kula school area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The map with the markings will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, marked map under Exhibit P2291 shall be assigned Exhibit P2548. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I see it's time for the break, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, I would agree. We must have our break now, and we will resume quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before we continue with Mr. Butler's testimony, the Chamber would like to issue an oral decision on the Prosecution's supplemental motion for leave to amend its Rule 65 ter exhibit list and witness list, filed on the 15th of June, 2011, whereby the Prosecution seeks leave to add 13 documents to its Rule 65 ter exhibit list and to amend its 65 ter witness list in order to expand the scope of Witness Blaszczyk's anticipated testimony and to add an additional individual to the list. Since the Prosecution may apply for protective measures for this individual, the Chamber will refer to this individual as Witness X. The Defence submitted a response to the motion on the 11th of July, and the English version was filed before the Chamber on the 13th of July, 2011. The Defence submitted that in principle, it did not object to the Prosecution's motion, on the condition that it be given sufficient time to analyse the proposed documents and prepare for the testimony and cross-examination of the two proposed witnesses. The Chamber has reviewed the 13 documents the Prosecution identified in its motion and which it seeks to add to the Rule 65 ter exhibit list. It has satisfied itself that the documents are of prima facie relevance and probative value to the charges against the accused. It notes, however, that three of these documents have, in fact, already been admitted into evidence. These are Exhibits P2427, through Witness Milomir Savcic, and the Exhibits 2515 and P2518, both through the current witness, Richard Butler. By this decision, the Chamber grants the Prosecution's request to add the remaining ten documents to the exhibit list. Further, the Chamber is of the view that it would be in the interests of justice to grant the Prosecution's request to add Witness X to the witness list and to expand the scope of Witness Blaszczyk's anticipated testimony. The anticipated evidence of Witness X concerns his position in the Main Staff Sector for Intelligence and Security and his relationship vis-a-vis the accused, as well as his involvement in the events relating to the disappearance of a victim named in the indictment. Witness Blaszczyk is expected to give evidence concerning the chain of custody of the documents added to the exhibit list by this decision. The Chamber has satisfied itself that such evidence is prima facie relevant to the charges against the accused, and hereby grants the Prosecution motion with regard to Witness X and Witness Blaszczyk. In order to ensure that the Defence has sufficient time to prepare for the upcoming testimony of the two witnesses and to review the documents the Prosecution intends to use with them, the Chamber directs the Prosecution that these witnesses be called at the end of the Prosecution case, following the last witness listed by the Prosecution in its submission of witnesses for the month of August, which was filed on the 15th of July, 2011. Having decided to grant the Prosecution's motion, the Chamber, nevertheless, would like to refer the Prosecution to its submission in court on the 4th of July, transcript page 15992, suggesting that there not be a need to recall Witness Blaszczyk. The Chamber leaves this matter in the hands of the Prosecution. And while it grants the Prosecution motion with regard to this witness, it welcomes any reduction of the remainder of the Prosecution's case. This concludes this decision. At this point in time, I would kindly ask Mr. McCloskey about the remainder of his examination-in-chief of the current witness, Mr. Butler. You have extended the estimated time by many, many hours already, and taking into account the length of the cross-examination of this witness by Mr. Tolimir, we need a new updated indication of the remaining time. For sure, we will not be able to finish with the testimony of this witness before the summer recess, but there can't be an unlimited time for the examination by both parties. Mr. McCloskey, can you give us an update? And before you respond, I would like to make one observation. You have, with some documents which are already in evidence, dealt with every word of, for instance, an intercept or another document. Perhaps you can reduce the topics and the matters raised with the witness in your examination. Up to now, you have used 22 hours and 11 minutes of your 15 hours indicated at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Thank you. As I'd mentioned the other day, my estimate was based on the Popovic testimony, and I'd reduced my documents from, I believe, about 230 in that to 190. And so the only thing I can think of is just the speed which we're going. Given that that's how many documents I have left [indicates], about an inch, it's important material right on point with the crimes and the activities of these times. I hope -- if I'm realistic, I should finish sometime tomorrow. I'm hoping that we finish sometime tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I was hoping you will be able to finish today.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Oh, I am so tired, I would love to finish today, Mr. President, and I will try to take into account what you're saying. And sometimes when I paraphrase, it's harder for the court reporter, and I don't want to leave out key items. But I will try to keep this as to the point as possible and hope to get through, but I just -- I can see the number of documents. I just don't see us being able to do that, but we'll give it our best try.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, I see you on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Defence encourages the Prosecution to use as much time as necessary for this witness. We are aware of the slowness of the process and why that is the case. The Defence, however, is going to insist on the equality of arms; i.e., the Defence will request the same number of hours for the cross-examination as was used for the examination-in-chief. We understand why this is lasting a long time. There are a lot of grounds to cover. In the Popovic case, there were a lot of stipulations and a lot of agreed facts. In this case, for understandable reasons, these things lack, and that is why this examination-in-chief is going to last, and we appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is exactly the reason for my concern. And, of course, we will, as I indicated earlier, protect the rights of the accused and observe the equality of arms. No doubt about that. But that will take us, I'm afraid, into the beginning of September with this witness. We have only one week in August left for hearings, perhaps one or two days more. But if I'm not mistaken, this is the eighth day of testimony of this witness, if it is not the ninth. I would kindly invite you, Mr. McCloskey, to shorten your examination as much as possible. Perhaps you can finish after the first session by tomorrow, if that is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I will try, Mr. President, but I can tell you the reason it's so slow is because I am speaking so slowly. It's completely unnatural for me. We would have been done in five days. I know that for a fact. That's why this is taking so long. And I have no problem with it, but please understand that. It's because we're going so slowly. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But we know that you are able to speak much more fast, I know that, but -- and we appreciate, for the sake of the interpreters and the court reporter, the speed you are talking.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, we have spoken briefly with Mr. Butler and the Court Officer so he is aware of that first day when we're back into court, and so the logistics of him coming back then are already in place. So we hope that that is where we're going to be able to take off. We're waiting to hear -- I think Mr. Butler's probably waiting to hear from the judges that are waiting for him in the United States and his employer, but that's the plan, and the Court Officer is helping us with that logistical issue so that he can come back and start right away and the general can get full cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The witness should be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, our apologies for the delayed start to the second session. We had to discuss some procedural matters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Also in relation to your testimony and the length of your stay here in The Hague. Mr. McCloskey, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Could we go now to 65 ter 839. It should be at 172 in the tab.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I can see you reviewing that, Mr. Butler. Can you tell us what this document is and how it relates to the previous conversation, if at all, in your view?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This particular document is related to the previous conversation, in so much that it represents the work and accounting of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade's technical services people and rear services organ to properly disburse 500 litres of D2 and to account for the remainder of it coming back to Colonel Popovic. As I've indicated in my prior testimony, the fact that people like Colonel Popovic or Colonel Beara or others were involved in unlawful acts, they were still operating within a military organisational bureaucracy, and that various rules and procedures with relation to fuel, technical services, and other equipment had to be followed and properly accounted for. So this particular document illustrates that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we can see at what is numbered Box 15, under "Addressee Station," that it's for Lieutenant Colonel Popovic; is that your understanding?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Box 15 says "KDK," commander of the Drina Corps, and then 15 states "Lieutenant Colonel Popovic."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the "Request Approved" box says "500," and do you tie that to the previous intercept?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Who, in your view, is the "Captain S. Milosevic" that is referred to in the middle of the page; do you recall?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Captain Milosevic is the assistant commander for Rear Services of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And we see, in the left-hand corner, it's handwritten "16 July 1995." That's clearly the date of the previous intercept. But at the bottom, we see handwritten "17 July." How do you account for that difference? Could this be a 17 July document and, therefore, not related to this intercept?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I take this as 16 July, related to the intercept. Again, it's a process that occurs. And one part of the accounting process occurred on 17 July, and there's a separate signature of an "M. Krstic" who is a Zvornik Brigade chief of Technical Services during this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I'd offer this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 839 shall be assigned Exhibit P2549. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And could we now go to P342.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please leave the document on the screen for a moment. Judge Nyambe has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: I'm a little bit lost. I can see the reference to what is in Box 14 and 15, and the "500 litres," and "Captain Milosevic," but I don't see the date, "16th July." Can you assist me to locate that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am. If you look at the very top lines, Box number 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you, I've got it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I've just noticed something. Translation of Column 8 [as interpreted], I believe, in the original, in Serbian, we have number "500," which is crossed out, but in translation that is not reflected correctly, or at least it looks like this number, "500," is crossed out. I don't know if that may be of some significance or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, if you allow me, I can go into greater detail with this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: My problem is that I don't find the Box 8 at the moment. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I said "28."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, can you explain to us, as best you can, your understanding of how this document works, especially in the amounts of fuel as they were noted and disbursed here, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Within this document, it notes, in Box 28, 500 litres requested/approved. You go down several lines, you will see a remark. Out of 500 litres, 140 litres were returned unused. So then in Box 29, as part of that accounting process, they're reflecting the total amount of fuel used or consumed, which is 360 litres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for your explanation. Now we should go to the next document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's an interesting balance, Mr. President. I will try to reach it. I know it's -- I have the same concern.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P342 is under seal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Butler, we see a 16 July intercept from 1615 hours, where they recorded a conversation between the Main Staff duty officer and General Mladic. And it says "General, who was inaudible." Who do you take that "who" to mean, based on what this says? Who is inaudible in this conversation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this context, I believe what they're saying is that General Mladic, they recognise that it's him, but they're not able to understand, for whatever reason, the conversation or the text of -- or the audio portion of what he's saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And we see here that in this one-sided conversation, where we can't hear the general, it says: "Good day, General, sir. "Well, it's like this. I've just sent a telegram to Toso." What do you think the Main Staff duty officer is talking about here, and who?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that he's referring to "Toso" as the nickname for General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And I won't read the entire text of this, but we see here that according to the duty officer, that the president called a while back and was informed by Karisik that Pandurevic had arranged the passage for Muslims over that territory. It talks about other things, doing it without authorisation, and I won't read all that out. But can you tell us, firstly, who do you think the president is in this and who is this Karisik?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Good afternoon to everyone. Could we have the reference for the claim that the "Toso" mentioned in this telegram is a reference to me? Is there any other indicator that would point in my direction, in view of the fact that this is a completely different theatre of war, not the one where I was ? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now you are giving evidence, Mr. Tolimir. You may deal with this question during your cross-examination because it was the answer of the witness. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, can you remind us why -- and tell us, in this conversation, why you believe -- or who you believe "Toso" is and why?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the investigation and interview of various VRS officials reflect, "Toso" was a nickname for General Tolimir. Given the context of the conversation between a Main Staff duty officer and General Mladic, both of whom would be, presumably, familiar with General Tolimir and his nickname, I conclude that they're referring to -- when they say "sending a telegram to Toso," they're referring to sending a telegram to General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did we just see, on the 15th of July, General Tolimir, aka Toso, sending out a telegram from the Rogatica area?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who do you think the president is in this context?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this context, I believe the president is President Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who do you think Karisik is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Karisik is the acting minister of the interior at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what, in your view, is being said -- I mean, what is going on here, from this one-sided conversation, in your view, and can you tie it to the events, as you know them, if you can?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The con -- again, I keep using the phrase "context," but it always is important to understand, when one looks at an intercept or an order, how it lays into the context of things that are happening on the ground. But as discussed earlier, Colonel Pandurevic at this time has made a decision to allow the Bosnian Muslim column to go into ABiH territory. This particular intercept reflects the fact that now the highest levels of the Republika Srpska, the president of the republic in this sense, have heard or have received indications that this is the case, and they are making their own inquiries to the army to try and ascertain what the actual situation is and whether or not Pandurevic has allowed the column to pass, and, if not, directions that he does nothing without seeking authorisation first.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And would this matter be something, in your view, that would be the subject of a telegram or -- to General Tolimir, even if he is in the Zepa theatre somewhere?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given the significance of this particular development, yes, sir, I believe it would.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The general knowledge of the operational goals with respect to what the military was doing with the column and what their plan was was to continue to militarily attack it in an effort to defeat it and destroy it, if practicable. The fact that a brigade commander would unilaterally allow what would be thousands of Muslim soldiers to retreat unmolested across his lines and into ABiH territory would have a significant military and political impact within the RS. These are, you know, issues of, obviously, high enough gravity that President Karadzic has found out about them, and using the phrase "through Karisik," it implies that the Ministry of the Interior, either the MUP police forces on the ground in Zvornik or the RDB internal security services have learned of this development and have rapidly apprised their political leadership of what the situation is. So given the seniority of both the political and military people who are trying to ascertain what the truth is, makes all the sense in the world that the senior intelligence officer and security officer for the VRS is going to be made aware of what the situation is and what steps are being taken to figure out what the truth is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we throw in the charged offences, and at the same time 1650 hours on the 16th, over a thousand people are being summarily executed at the Branjevo Farm, and burial operations are going on at Kozluk and Petkovci and Orahovac, would this complication referred to have other implications that the chief of security would need to know about?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I quite understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Does this action that -- the complications of opening the column and potential resources that it may involve, could that interfere or affect the ability to carry out the murder operation in some way or would it be something that the murder -- people conducting the murder operation would want to know about, as they are doing it in this area, in the same area around Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In terms of timing, if that's what you're leading to, by this particular time, most -- at 1615, most everyone has already been executed. There may, at this late hour, still be some people left in the Dom of Culture, but by this time most of the actual executions at all of these sites are completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Are these people that have been executed or are in the process of being executed people that came, in large part, from this column that is being let through?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. All of these people were individuals that were either taken into custody at Potocari on the 12th or 13th or those who were subsequently captured by the VRS at places like Nova Kasaba, Konjevic Polje, and the Bratunac-Konjevic Polje road on -- you know, beginning the 12th through, potentially, the 14th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It was a poorly-framed question. I didn't mean they were taken at Baljkovica. I meant that they are the same -- are they the same group that fled from Srebrenica, aside from the Potocari people?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Those were the people from the column who were captured on the 12th, 13th, and 14th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And were there efforts to continue to execute people that were captured from the column on the days after the 16th, 17th, 18th?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. There were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think you've discussed those, so I don't need to repeat that. And this is already in evidence, so I'll go on. If we could go to P1089. And we see that this is an interim combat report from the Zvornik Brigade in the name of Vinko Pandurevic. I won't read it all. Can you just tell us -- paraphrase briefly what this says and how it fits into your analysis. I think you've talked about it quite a bit, so I don't think we need too much more information on it. Can you just give us the guts of this as we're looking over it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, paragraph 1 lays out the situation that he's facing militarily -- that he believes he's facing militarily from the column, including references to what he believes are the size of the column as well as the ferocity of the attacks that the column is undertaking against his subordinate units. The second paragraph lays out what his units are trying to accomplish and over what particular areas of terrain, and whether they've been successful, as well as the casualties they've been taking. In paragraph 3, he lays out, as a result of the consequences that are occurring, the decision that he has made to open a corridor along the line for the column to escape.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. In paragraph 3, we see he says: "I have decided, in view of the situation, to open a corridor along the line of three trenches for the civilian population - about 5.000 of them." Is there ever a mention in this document that he's also let through army or able-bodied men?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. In a very off-handed way, if one looks at the continuation of paragraph 3, he seeks to -- and it's on the English language second page. He seeks to kind of hold open the abstract prospect that there's certain a number of soldiers that got out among the civilians. He is clearly at this stage trying to avoid -- clearly stating the reality, which is that obviously both the soldiers and the civilians accompanying the column have been let through by down-playing the issue of how many soldiers his action has allowed to escape.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This comment in paragraph 6: "I consider that the Krivaja 95 operation is not complete as long as a single enemy soldier or civilian remains behind the front-line." What do you make of that reference, especially to the "civilian" here?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this, he's referring to the idea that once these lines close again, he has an awareness that it's not going to be the complete column. There will still be hundreds of stragglers that are roaming throughout the territory of a number of the battalions, the 4th, the 6th, and the 7th, who aren't going to be able to make it through the lines within the 24-hour specified time-frame. So he's already thinking ahead, as part of 6, his future proposals as to what he's going to need to -- once the lines are re-established after the end of the cease-fire, to complete the job that he's doing against those military and civilian personnel who, for whatever reason, would not be able to escape through the lines on the 16th and the morning and afternoon of the 17th, the period of the cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to 65 ter 3020B. This is a -- I'm sure you know, an intercept that you have spoken about many times. 16 July, 2116 hours: "Palma, from Lieutenant Colonel Vujadin Popovic, to Rasic, the Operations Centre, and Lieutenant Colonel Popovic asked to be connected with General Krstic at Zlatar, and he was not there, so he asked to be connected to the Operations Centre." Do you recall, Mr. Butler, from earlier in the day who the duty officer was at the Vlasenica Drina Corps headquarters?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was an officer named Rasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That would be correct. And would that be consistent with this intercept?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It's someone in the duty operations officer [sic] who would be picking up the phone and engaging conversations; yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we see that Popovic says: "Hello, Lieutenant Colonel Popovic speaking." And then Rasic says: "Rasic here, can I help you?" And Popovic says: "Rale?" Rasic says: "Yes." Popovic: "I was just up there." "Yes." "I was with the boss personally." "Yes." "Here where I am ... you know where I am?" "I know." "Well, you got his interim report." What, in your view, is this a reference to? Where -- when he says I was just up there, and "the boss personally"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that when he says this, he's referring to the commander of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade, Colonel Pandurevic, and the interim report he discusses is the interim combat report that Colonel Pandurevic sent to the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
