utterances.text: That's the one we just looked at?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when he says: "I was just up there," where do you think he means?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this particular context, I believe he's referring to the forward command post of the Zvornik Brigade, where Colonel Pandurevic normally would be located during this battle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you explain to us how you've come to those conclusions? Is there any other materials to indicate -- to help you reach that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Again, through the course of the investigation, several of the phrases, "up there," "where they are," and things of that nature are described. I'm aware Obrenovic has given some descriptions of them, other officers of the Zvornik Brigade who were interviewed, who explain where Colonel Pandurevic was and what he was doing on these certain days, so again in that part it's constructive analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you recall any documents or intercepts where Popovic was requested to go in a particular place that we haven't dealt with in your testimony thus far?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm finding I'm blanking out at the moment. I don't believe so. My memory might have to be refreshed on that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Do you remember that -- was there any ever a point where the Drina Corps had heard about the column or the quarter being opened up, and they were out of touch with Vinko Pandurevic and were trying to get in touch with him some way?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I do recall that there is an intercept that's attributed to the Drina Corps where they are also seeking information from Colonel Pandurevic, or the Zvornik Brigade even in general, to try and get confirmation as to what is occurring on the ground on 16 July specifically related to rumours that Colonel Pandurevic is allowing the column to go through.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you remember a reference to Popovic being ordered to go there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I vaguely do. I just -- I don't remember the entire text of the intercept right off the top of my head, regrettably.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No problem. Let's look at the rest of it. Popovic says: "It's all just like he wrote ... I was there on the spot and saw for myself he had received some numbers ... well, that's not even important ... I'll come there tomorrow, so tell the general ... I've finished the job." What do you think he's referring to there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe in this particular passage of the intercept, Colonel Popovic is referring to two separate things. First, he's verifying that the situation and the gravity of the situation, as described by Colonel Pandurevic in his report, is accurate. And when he's talking about receiving numbers, he is referring to reinforcements that arrived to the unit through the course of the day and acknowledging that they've been received as scheduled. The last phrase, however, where he says, "I've finished the job," I believe that he's referring to his particular job, which is the completion of the execution of the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And we see some other back and forth, and then he says: "Well, in general terms, there weren't any major problems. But up there, there were horrible problems, and that thing the commander sent, it was just the right thing." Then Rasic says: "Good." And he says: "Just the thing ... horrible ... it was horrible." What is your interpretation of those sentences?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I first discussed this particular intercept during the Krstic case, it was my conclusion that when he was using the phrase "up there," he was talking up north in a geographic sense. Subsequent to that testimony and during later testimony in other cases, after hearing from Dragan Obrenovic referring to the same thing, what Colonel Obrenovic at the time explained, and which makes more sense, is that when they are talking about geographic terms "up" and "down," what they are referring to in this context is within the Zvornik Brigade, the terrain as it slopes from the low ground near Zvornik and the Drina River to the higher ground, where the IKM and the battle-fields were. So in this context, it's more appropriate to read it, when he says "up there," he's talking about "up there" in the sense of the forward command post and where the battle-fields were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So -- but you didn't tell us when you first saw this and talked about it in Krstic, what did you think the "horrible" was a reference to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding was the "horrible" was a reference to the scope of the executions that had occurred in Pilica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And now what is your view on that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the scope of the situation at the battle-field of Baljkovica, Memici, and those places where many Bosnian Serb soldiers were killed or wounded because of the fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And if we could go to the next page in the English and the next page in the B/C/S, we see a reference to Rasic asked: "Tell me, did anything arrive there from Vidoje Blagojevic?" And then they talk about manpower, and Popovic says: "Yes, it did arrive, but it wasn't brought in on time, and that's why the commander had big problems." Then there's a question: "When exactly did Blagojevic's men arrive?" And we can read the rest, that Rasic tells him, Okay, find out exactly when they arrived and call back. Now, can you tell us, what was your first analysis and testimony about what this meant in the Krstic case, and have you changed your view from that, and why?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. As the background context of the executions at Branjevo Farm, the testimony of Drazen Erdemovic notes that in the morning hours or during the first parts of the execution, that they were undertaken by members of the 10th Sabotage Unit, and that at some point later on in the afternoon, that men or soldiers from Bratunac took over completing the executions at Branjevo, and after that point the 10th Sabotage went into Pilica, to the local cafe. As the investigation continued and as more intercepts became available and other information became available, it became clear, at least to me, that in this particular context of the intercept, what they were referring to was a group of soldiers that was sent from the Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade into the Zvornik Brigade area, at the request of Colonel Pandurevic, for reinforcements for the battle-front, and that they're not referring to people sent for the execution. So based off the additional new information, I changed my analysis of what this particular intercept means to reflect the fact that the people arriving from Blagojevic were not those people who were at Branjevo, executing people, but were instead individuals who were sent and committed into combat operations at some time on the afternoon of 16 July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's -- and I believe I need to offer that into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 3020B shall be assigned Exhibit P2550. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to 3021A. It's the next, and this is 10 minutes after the last one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It should be 3021A.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And as we see, it's 2126 hours; participants, Colonel Cerovic and the Palma duty officer. And if we recall that Rasic says: "Okay. Find out exactly and call me back," when he's asking about when Blagojevic's men arrive. Did this intercept have anything to do with your revised analysis of the previous intercept?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, in the sense that after that particular conversation, there's a subsequent conversation between the Palma duty officer and Colonel Cerovic from the Drina Corps, where he is informed in more specific detail about reinforcements coming from Badem, the telephonic code-name for the Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade, as well as additional members of various MUP companies that arrive from other locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this information that men arrived from Badem at 1705 hours, is that consistent or not consistent with what Erdemovic said about the time that they arrived, if you can recall?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be inconsistent, because Erdemovic has testified that it would be before 1705 hours. I don't believe Erdemovic said they were anywhere this late. I think they arrived more along the lines of 1300.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd offer that into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, it will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 3021A shall be assigned Exhibit P2551. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And could we now go to 65 ter 4051.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this should be looked at in conjunction with the following document, P394B and P2207, Mr. Butler, for your review. But we now have a handwritten document that I believe was retrieved from the Drina Corps collection, and we see that in the right-hand corner, it's handwritten and underlined: "Informed by Tolimir." It's dated 16 July 1995. It has a number, 04/2-30, and it says: "Sator for Uran and Elektron." And then we see what it is talking about. On 16 July, 0300 hours, Muslim armed group attacked UN OPs at various places. Do you have any knowledge what "Sator for Uran and Elektron" is right now, Mr. Butler?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not specifically. I'm aware that just as the Bratunac -- or just as the brigades had telephonic code-names, they also had code-names that were assigned to them as part of the tactical-level communications radio network. When I say "tactical communications," I'm talking the battle-field communications, the smaller radios mostly in the VHF range, that were used as another means of controlling and keeping abreast of what was happening at the actual battle sites. If I recall correctly, "Uran" is the Drina Corps one. But it's been many years since I've seen the actual communications plan, so I can't be sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that is in evidence, so that's something we can refer to. And looking at the second page in English, again it talks a bit more about people at the UN base and in the elementary school in Zepa. We need to go over in the B/C/S. And it talks about Muslims taking over other observation posts: "Through the UN commander who is in our territory, we called the Muslims to leave. We'll call them to gather all their men and civilians at the UN base in Zepa." What does this have to do with?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: From reading it, it looks like a battle-field report, something that would ultimately be incorporated into a daily or interim combat report from a particular unit, discussing the situation on 16 July related to Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If General Tolimir was still in the position of the -- in the Zepa area, would this be the kind of information he may have been aware of or be able to pass on to someone, as this note says: "Informed by Tolimir"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I presume he would.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'd offer this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 4051 shall be assigned Exhibit P2552. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And could we go to P394B, which we see is an intercept. It's also dated 16 July. The time is 1000 hours. It's between Mico and Toso. Who do you think Mico and Toso are, as you review this intercept?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe "Toso," again, is a nickname for General Tolimir. I'm not sure that I can lay out who "Mico" would be in this context.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And if General Tolimir said in this, I sent you you know what over there via Uran and you send it to me via Uran because this one is not secure. If Uran is, in fact, the Drina Corps IKM for an operation, what is Tolimir saying here?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Basically, he's indicating that information sent to him should be -- basically go through that particular headquarters and he will send his information to that particular headquarters, because he recognises that this particular communications channel is not secure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Does this suggest he knows there is a communication channel that is secure?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you recall, when Tolimir says: "And to tell Pepo," do you recall that nickname at all?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's been a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And we see that it continues on, where General Tolimir says that: "... I received what he sent me, and if he wants to send me something, he can call Uran on the same line that you are communicating with Uran, and he can relay the telegram for me through it, and you know my call sign." If --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. Tolimir just informed me, and I was going through my papers here, but -- and I can follow what Mr. McCloskey is saying, but I don't see it on the monitor. And I believe that in Serbian, it should be on the following page, on page 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that, and of course it's also the hard copy should be in your binder. I hope everyone has the binders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, if Colonel Salapura identified himself as "Pepo," would that be consistent with this intercept?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It certainly -- given the fact that we're talking about General Tolimir, and Salapura is one of his subordinates, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It goes on, and I won't read all of it, but General Tolimir talks about sending a telegram that they were supposed to receive through Uran. M says he didn't receive it yet and he's going to call him now. And then they go on and continue to talk a bit more about telegrams, and Tolimir ends up saying at the end: "Call him and then tell Pepo he can send telegrams this way, and I can send it to them." Now, this part at the bottom: "Five minutes later Mico called Jevdo on this frequency and asked about two telegrams he was supposed to forward him. They agreed that Jevdo was going to send them immediately?" Do you remember Jevdo or a person by the name of Jevdo that may have been involved in communications?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It would be Milenko Jevdjevic, who was the communications officer for the Drina Corps and who, I'm also aware from his previous statement and testimony, was at the Drina Corps IKM during the military operations related to Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. And if we can now go to P2207.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is another handwritten document, and this time it's got up in the left-hand corner "Command of the Drina Corps IKM Krivace," and it's dated the 17th, the next day, from what we've just seen, and it talks about a radio conversation with Avdo Palic. And I won't go into the details of that, but it's -- this radio conversation was reported by General Tolimir. What is your view of -- we now see General Tolimir addressing a document like this, where previously, I think you'll recall, we saw documents from the 1st Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade or -- can you make anything out about where General Tolimir would be or anything related to the previous two documents which involve the Drina Corps IKM? What, if anything, can you -- can you help us out with on this, Mr. Butler?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: While it's not clear what his precise location is, it does reflect the fact that wherever General Tolimir is physically located, that it's been determined that for passing messages and information back and forth, the closest proximity between where General Tolimir might be and a secure means of communication is going to be the Drina Corps IKM.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now let's go to P378A. We'll skip a document. We're now at 181, tab 181, P378A. It's from the 17th, 1244 hours, X and Trbic. Trbic answers: "Yes, can I help you?" X says: "Tell me, is Pop there?" Trbic says: "No." "You don't know where he is?" "Well, he went there to -- towards that task." X says: "North of you?" What is your viewpoint, as we read down through this intercept? What is going on here?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this discussion, "Pop," being Colonel Popovic, somebody is looking for Colonel Popovic. He's speaking with Trbic, who is the assistant to Drago Nikolic as a security officer, and Trbic is explaining that Popovic is not physically here, "here" being the location the Zvornik Brigade headquarters at Standard, and indicating that he's dealing with a task north. Or X actually asks the question, North of you, and Trbic confirms that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the previous document, P552A indicated that Trbic identified himself as the duty officer. So can you tell us what the investigation, in your view, of documents has borne out that was going on north of where Trbic was on 17 July that Popovic may have been involved -- or "Pop" may have been involved in?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. They were still continuing or finishing burial activity at Rocevic as well as burial activity at Branjevo Farm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And we see there's a request by X for Pop to get in touch with him. X says: "I know it is. Drago told me." Sorry, but -- Trbic says: "But it's very hard for me to do that." And X says: "I know it is, Drago told me, but ... I don't think of it that way." What do you take that to mean?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's talking about physically getting in touch with Colonel Popovic. The nearest phone line or secure phone line, military one, would go to the 1st Battalion headquarters, which is not near Branjevo, so in order for anybody to get in touch with Colonel Popovic at Branjevo, they're going to either have to take a vehicle and drive directly to where he is, or they're going to have to relay a message through wherever the nearest battalion or other military installation is that's connected to a switchboard. So it's just reflecting the fact that wherever Colonel Popovic is, he is not near or he does not have ready access to a phone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to the next document, P379A. It's just five minutes later. It's X and Trbic. X says, It's changed again, and to get in touch with him and let him finish that work. What does this mean, to your -- in your view, briefly?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whoever has been looking for Colonel Popovic has changed their mind and now decided that rather than immediately have Popovic report to them or him, that he wants Popovic to complete the work that he's doing, and then only after he's done, he can then report back to whom he needs to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to the next document, 65 ter 3043. This is this same day, but at 1622 hours. It's between -- 3043A, 1622 hours, between Popovic and Y. And I won't read it all. We just hear that: "Popovic: Hello, it's Popovic, boss ... everything is okay ... that job is done ... everything's okay." "No problems," and gets an A, an A, the grade is an A, everything is okay, and: "Bye." Who -- what, in your view, is Popovic talking about at this point, and who would he be talking to and referring to as "boss," in your view?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my view, the fact that he's used the phrase "boss" reflects the fact that he is speaking to his immediate commander, which in this case would be General Major Krstic, the Drina Corps commander. He talks about at the place that he was at that base, so I infer that to mean that where he is at the moment he's having this conversation is at the Zvornik Brigade headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you know or recall what the investigation revealed about this small note at the bottom, where the interpreter heard French being heard in the background? Sorry, the intercept operator noted that: "French is heard in the background."

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that that was an issue that the investigation did look into. I don't recall what the results would be, off-hand, of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I'd offer that into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, it will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 3043A shall be assigned Exhibit P2553. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can we go to 65 ter 1780. And, Mr. President, the next series of documents has to do with a particular section in the -- a crime charged in the indictment. I believe we've referred to it as the Nezuk executions. So it does get a little bit lost in the maze, but this is a specific reference, as we'll get to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We see a Main Staff document from 15 July, from General Miletic, talking about the dispatch of a unit to the 1st Zvornik Brigade from the 1st Krajina Corps. Can you briefly explain this and how that fit in, if you can recall, to what was going on at the time, just briefly?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Once the senior leadership of the Drina Corps and the Main Staff recognised the gravity of the military situation developing in Zvornik during the evening hours of 14 July, there were a number of actions that were done where various military and police units that could be readily made available were ordered to go to the zone of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade and were placed under the command of Colonel Pandurevic for the duration of those military operations. This particular document reflects one company of the 1st Krajina Corps being made available as part of the general reinforcements.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I'd offer that into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 3043A -- oh, pardon me -- 1780 shall be assigned Exhibit P2554. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we now go to 65 ter 388.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is a document from the 1st Krajina Corps, by its commander, ordering that a unit go to the Zvornik Brigade. Is that consistent with the previous document and what you know about the investigation? Did they actually go?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it is consistent. And, yes, sir, this unit actually did deploy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if we could go to P14 -- I'm sorry, that -- I'd offer that into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: 65 ter 388 will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 388 shall be assigned Exhibit P2555. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And to try to save a little time: Mr. Butler, we see from the next tab it's a section from P1459, page 109, that there is a note in the Zvornik Brigade duty officer note-book about -- that men from the 16th Krajina are at TT602 and that Obrenovic should be informed. What is a "TT602"? The interpreters told us "trig point."

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. On maps, military or civilian, there are established points on the ground that correspond to points on the map that are often used for surveying. In this particular context, they've -- often they're hills or other locations, but in this particular one, he's basically using -- rather than exactly identifying where the unit is, he's basically saying they're at a certain trigonometric point, it's probably Hill 602 or Trig Point 602. I mean, it's a fixed location on a map.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's break time, Mr. President, and we're getting -- we're getting closer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have on the screen both versions in English, and I believe the Serbian transcript should be on page 108.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That's correct. Thank you very much. No, it's the wrong page. [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't really think it's necessary, frankly. I was trying to save some time, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But during the break, somebody may look at it. We must have our second break, and we'll resume quarter past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Could we go to 65 ter 322.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is a combat report from the Zvornik Brigade of 19 July 1995, under the name of Vinko Pandurevic. Now, I just -- in paragraph 2 of this, it talks about: "All available units (POSS, a company of the 16th Krajina ..." Can you relate this reference to the 16th Krajina to the unit we've been talking about that was sent to Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, this is that unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I'd offer this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 322 shall be assigned Exhibit P2556. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can we go to 65 ter 2215. And this is a Main Staff report to the president. If we could go to the Drina Corps section. It should be page 4 in the English, and it's paragraph 6 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I take it this is behind tab 192.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. We've skipped ahead a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And there's a reference in here that: "At 1930 hours, we received information that the enemy were building rafts in the Crni Potok sector, escaping to the right Drina bank." 31 July, Muslims going over rafts to the right-side bank of the Drina, what do you connect this to, if you recall, Mr. Butler?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you were going a little bit too fast for me. What are we -- where are you in this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We went to 31 -- we're in 31 July.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: At the Drina Corps, page 4. We now have Muslims building rafts and going across the Drina. And you can look into the couple of intercepts after that that you would have reviewed along with this document, if you remember.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, in this particular context, after the fall of the Zepa enclave, several thousand Bosnian Muslim soldiers from the former 28th Division sought -- rather than to put themselves in the custody of the VRS, they broke out first over land, but actually in a direction that would bring them to Serbia. So there was a concerted effort to break out across the Drina River and then ultimately place themselves in the custody of the Government of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And I would offer this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 2215 shall be assigned Exhibit P2557. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And could we go to P345.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is a confidential document and should not be broadcast. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is an intercept from August 1st, with a person named Jevtic from Serbia, and Stevo, and Ljubisa Beara from the Main Staff. And again I won't go over this, but we see that Stevo is saying: "Listen, why do you let these Turks swim towards you?" And if we go on to the second page in the English, they continue to talk on that subject. And S says: "And do keep in touch. Beara is going to call you." And then as we go down, we -- to the third page in English, we see: "Hello, good morning. Ljubo Beara speaking." And they're talking about -- we see: "Let me tell you," is this what -- this person, J, is telling to Beara. "... we and our blue guys, what we catch, we process. And if they're interested, we hand them over." What do you think there -- Beara is talking about here with this person?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Beara is talking about a process by which individuals who've crossed the Drina River and who are in FRY territory, about how the FRY might turn some of those people back over to the Republika Srpska, and, in fact, as it's listed here, notice that they've already done that on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to the next document, which is 65 ter 3208A. We're now on August 2nd, and it's another intercept between someone they called Mandzuka and General Krstic. And again we see that Mandzuka is saying: "We just have a few down in the creek. Some of them have gone through, about a thousand of them." Krstic says: "You shouldn't have let any of them escape." Then: "We didn't dare to cross over into the other state. We just checked the terrain by helicopter yesterday. It's pretty inaccessible. Did you see how the Serbian ministers accepted them over like liberators? Even the Red Cross came." And look at the rest of that, and it talks about 2.000 -- Beara went over there to Serbia. He'll take care if there's some captured and dead. They threw away their weapons. What's this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is, at this point in time, a reflection that General Krstic and whomever Mandzuka is are discussing their displeasure about the fact that various individuals in Serbia have made decisions that they're not going to immediately turn Bosnian Muslims from Zepa back over to the Republika Srpska. In fact, they're treating them in accordance with established international law, and the Red Cross is given access to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I'll offer that into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, it will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 3208A shall be assigned Exhibit P2558. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now we're at P528B.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is a still August 2nd intercept, 1240 hours, between Krstic and Popovic. We see Krstic talking to Popovic and saying: "Go over to Bajina Basta, you and Kosoric. You know what you have to do." Remind us where Bajina Basta is and who Kosoric is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bajina Basta is a town on the Serbian side, and "Kosoric" is Svetozar -- in this context, I believe it is Svetozar Kosoric, who is the chief of intelligence for the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we see, two-thirds of the way down, Popovic says: "He went up there because we had some parcels, to check what they know." What do you think that's a reference to? Again, we hear this term "parcels."

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. And again "parcels" being a reference to prisoners. "To check what they know" is a cryptic reference, or maybe not so cryptic, to interrogating them for information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. We now go to P529C, still 2 August.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is Popovic and X, Boss Krle. And we see what Popovic is saying to Krstic, that: "Well, Beara just called me. He came back from there this morning." He says: "He gave the report to Miletic." Who would that "Miletic" be, in your view?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be General Major Miletic, the chief of operations of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Then we see that Popovic says: "There are 500 to 600 of them ..." What do you think he's referring to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suspect in this context, what he's referring to is at least one group of individuals who are in custody of the FRY in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Then as we look down, there's a mention of Kosoric to go to Bajina Basta. And as we look at what X -- who do you believe X is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Krle is a nickname for General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And he tells Popovic: "And I want you to bring the Turks back ... to me. Is that clear, man?" And Popovic says: "What if they won't give them?" Krstic: "What do you mean, they won't give them?" "Well, they won't give them, they won't give them." Krstic says: "They're our Turks, man." Popovic says: "Well, the MUP won't allow access ..." Krstic ends up saying: "I'll turn the gun barrels on them. Did you understand me?" What's Krstic saying here?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Krstic is laying out the fact that he is not pleased about the fact that the Serbian -- or the FRY Ministry of Interior will not permit the VRS to take custody of these Bosnian Muslims who are currently in the FRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, that series of intercepts, beginning with that report to the president, we see that Beara and Popovic and Kosoric are mentioned several times in this. Would this be the kind of activity that General Tolimir would be briefed on, given that those, as we know, were his men involved in this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, the fact that reports are being given to Miletic, those will obviously be passed to General Tolimir, and it's expected that Colonel Popovic would keep General Tolimir apprised of -- I'm sorry, Colonel Beara would keep General Tolimir apprised of his dealings with the Serbian MUP and other authorities in the FRY pertaining to the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, can we go to -- it's 65 ter 40, but I -- I think this is in evidence already. But just perhaps we can check that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But as we're doing that, Mr. Butler, can you take a look at this 65 ter 40.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: For the record, this is Exhibit P2281. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. So that's not a problem, and I won't -- I think that's self-explanatory and it's been spoken to. How about 65 ter 41.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Butler, having in mind what you have seen in the tab, which is the last P document that we just mentioned - it's under 197, which is this fuel to go to Milorad Trbic, signed in Ratko Mladic's name - now let's look at this other document that same date. It's under the name of Colonel Zarko Ljubojecic, and notes: "Pursuant to the order of the commander of the Main Staff, immediately issue the following quantity of fuel." And is that related to the previous document of fuel going to Milorad Trpic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if we look at -- is there such a person Milorad Trpic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in the Zvornik Brigade, no. I don't believe anyone in the Drina Corps has that name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who would that be, Captain Milorad Trpic, in your view?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be Captain Milorad Trbic, who is the deputy security officer for the Zvornik Brigade. He is subordinate to Drago Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What does it say to you, if anything, that a security officer of the Zvornik Brigade is put in charge of such a large amount of fuel in mid-September 1995?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given the context of other information that I'm aware of, the fuel that is being used here, the special engineering tasks that are being discussed, relates to the effort that lasted for almost a month, month and a half, to exhume the primary grave-sites associated with the Srebrenica executions and the effort to remove those remains to more remote locations in and around the Zvornik area, some of them -- or many of them in relatively remote locations, in an effort to hide the evidence of the mass executions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: There's evidence in this case that Milorad Trbic was involved with this, that Vujadin Popovic was involved with this, that Momir Nikolic was involved with this. In your view, is there any way that General Tolimir would not have been knowledgeable and involved with this process of reburials?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. Given the gravity of the political impact that the discovery of the mass executions had when they were laid out at the United Nations Security Council back in August of 1995, and the implications thereof for both the political and military aspects of what was happening in the RS at the time, I can't believe that an effort like this, to essentially exhume all the remains and hide them in order to attempt to conceal the crime being conducted by a number of security officers from the Drina Corps, would somehow occur without the bare minimum knowledge of General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, yesterday General Tolimir objected -- I'm sorry, that one I've forgotten has not been into evidence, so I would offer that second fuel document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 41 shall be assigned Exhibit P2559. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yesterday, you testified that you believe Milan Stankovic was a member of the intelligence and security branch of the Main Staff, and I want to take you to the 2 May 2011 testimony of Petar Salapura at page 13475 to 13476, where he was asked the question: "Can you briefly name for us the people that worked under you in the Intelligence Administration in 1995? We're especially concerned about July 1995." He names various people, including Karanovic, Radoslav Jankovic, Slobodan Momlic. Then he says: "And sometime in June, Milovan Stankovic joined the administration. He was reassigned to us." Should Petar Salapura know the assignment of Milovan Stankovic [Realtime transcript read in error "Milo Stanic"] in the Main Staff intel branch in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. He obviously should know who is working for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And on the same topic, I'd like to go to the interview/statement of a man named Dusko Vukotic that was taken on September 17th, 2001. And I have a new ERN of -- excuse me, a new 65 ter number of 7455.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I for a moment ask you and draw your attention to page 74, line 2. You said: "Should Petar Salapura know the assignment of ...," and can you repeat, Mr. McCloskey, the name? Here we see "Stanic." Did you say "Stanic" or "Stankovic"?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I meant to say "Stankovic, Milovan Stankovic."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So I would like to take you to page 106 of his interview/statement back in 2001, which -- page 2 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And this is one of the documents which are not yet on the 65 ter exhibit list?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, this is specifically in response to General Tolimir's concern about Mr. Butler's conclusion regarding the job of Milan Stankovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I take it the Defence normally has no objection to add these documents to the 65 ter exhibit list. Is that correct, Mr. Gajic?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Every document that can help shed some light will not be objected to. However, there may be a miscommunication somewhere. Perhaps it has to do with a transcript. My apologies. I didn't get a chance to read it through over again. Now, the objection was not whether this was in the unit of Republika Srpska that was mentioned. It was in a different context. It had to do with the individuals who were in the Main Staff while they were assigned to Srebrenica and whether at that particular time they were under the command of Zdravko Tolimir. So I don't think what is at issue here is whether Milo Stankovic was a member of the Intelligence Administration or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for that, although it was slightly beyond the limit of the scope of matters you should address the Chamber with. On the other hand, leave is granted to add it to the 65 ter exhibit list. Mr. McCloskey, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I just want to make a reference to a section of this interview, which should be up on the -- page 3 in the B/C/S, page 2 in the English. All right, it's the bottom of page 2 in English. It looks like line 19. First of all, can you tell us, before we get to what Dusko Vukotic says, do you remember who Dusko Vukotic is or was at the time of July 1995?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Dusko Vukotic was the head of intelligence for the Zvornik Infantry Brigade in July of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And we see that Dean Manning asked Mr. Vukotic -- he's referring to a 17th July document, where there's three officers from the Main Staff, and I think we'll all agree that that's the 17 July document where he's mentioned. And Dusko Vukotic says: "I didn't see any of them, but on the 17th, whether I heard him on the radio communication, Milovan Stankovic, that even he spoke to Muminovic, Semso." Is that the proper name, Semso Muminovic, of a person you tried to say earlier?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, and he is the ABiH 2 Corps officer who was on the radio first with Colonel Pandurevic, and later with others, dealing with negotiating the cease-fire to allow the column to go out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Then Mr. Vukotic goes on to say: "I heard him on the communication, and I know his voice because he worked at the time in the Intelligence Administration of the Main Staff of the VRS ..." Now, does that also support your conclusion that Milovan Stankovic was a member of the intelligence branch of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. And, in fact, given that Dean Manning and I were here at roughly the same time, this might have even, in fact, been the first indication in my mind that would support that. I am aware that after I left, interviews and the testimony of Salapura were done that I was not a party to. But, again, I can't go back and tell you exactly what documents I know at this particular time or what references I'm aware of that would support my position, but clearly, you know, I do believe that he is an officer who was part of the intelligence staff there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And also in response to what Mr. Gajic just said: As a member of the intel unit of the Main Staff, what is his relationship to General Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in this particular context, his immediate supervisor would be Colonel Salapura, as the chief of intelligence. The next higher-up person within his chain would be General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I would offer those two-page sections and only those two pages of Dusko Vukotic's testimony into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Perhaps there are three pages, but the page numbers are indicated in your list of documents. They will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 7455 shall be assigned Exhibit P2560. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Butler, if we go back more days than I can remember now to your discussion of documents related to convoy -- convoy approvals, convoy restrictions, do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And in your binder of convoy materials, there was several documents related to convoy materials that I didn't specifically ask you about; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall that there's a group of them that I do not believe that we got to as part of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And have you been able to review those documents, as they were in your binder and associated with the other documents?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. And in that context, I've testified about many convoy-related documents in the Popovic case, and any documents in this particular case that I reviewed that weren't in the Popovic case, there should be proofing notes on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And those documents that were in your binder that you had prepared for, do they basically fit into your basic theory and analysis related to the convoy system and the convoy restrictions that you've been talking about?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. They're generally illustrations or examples of how the convoy process worked, how it was reviewed by various officers at the Main Staff, how particular pieces of cargo were approved, or how in many cases it was either not approved or cargos were reduced. And as I've testified before, I believe they're all in support of the plan that was laid out under Directive 7 with respect to the enclaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, it's my proposal that I provide you tomorrow with the list of those few remaining documents and offer them into evidence, based on the foundation that Mr. Butler has laid by his specific discussion of specific documents, and by what he just said, and from, I think, your understanding and my viewpoint that these convoy documents are, on their face, self-explanatory. And that I know the Trial Chamber generally wants a document referred to specifically prior to entering it into evidence, but I think in this -- perhaps in this particular situation, I would offer them into evidence in this context to get your ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Are you able to -- now, first of all, I take it these are documents contained in Binder number 2?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Absolutely, they are in Binder number 2. I skipped around a little bit, as you saw. And so to be perfectly clear, it would be best if I could give you those numbers tomorrow. But they're all in Binder number 2, and I can identify them very clearly tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It would be helpful for the Chamber and for the Defence if you can provide us the numbers of these documents so that we can prepare a decision on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. This --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I mean to provide us with the numbers by e-mail sometime during the morning of tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's precisely what Ms. Stewart said, and that will not be difficult. And one other topic I just recalled by looking at the Court Officer. I'm told that Mr. Butler has requested to have transcripts of his testimony to be able to review prior to his cross-examination, so I -- and there is also some, as you'll remember, some -- a small amount of confidential material. I've mentioned this to Mr. Gajic, but I -- Gajic, and I just pass that on to you for your decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The transcript is a public document, accessible for the public. Is there any objection for the Defence? Perhaps it supports the conduct of cross-examination. What is your position, Mr. Gajic?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I've already shared my opinion with Mr. McCloskey and told him exactly what you told us. We do not object to Mr. Butler receiving the transcript from this trial. Transcripts are public documents, and I really don't see why Mr. Butler should not be allowed to peruse them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: After having considered the situation with Mr. Registrar, your request is granted. Some parts of this transcript are confidential. I think nobody has any concern about giving you also this part of the transcript because you were present at that time. We were in private session for some minor matters, but you should be reminded that you are not allowed to publish these parts of the confidential transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That will not be a problem, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The Registrar is hereby instructed to provide you with a transcript of your testimony up to now. Thank you very much. Anything else, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, thank everyone, thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions for Mr. Butler, and we'll just provide you with those numbers tomorrow. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We will deal with these documents tomorrow, at the beginning of the session in the afternoon at 2.15 in this courtroom, and then Mr. Tolimir may commence his cross-examination. We adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 20th day of July, 2011, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.58 p.m.,
